content.title: About
content.content: Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia) is a juicy fruit with crisp flesh and a sweet‑tart flavor. It is eaten fresh and also used in desserts, salads, and marinades. The fruits are usually small, with smooth skin covered by a thin waxy film.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Japan the Asian pear is called “nashi,” while in China it is known as “shika.”
Unlike European pears, Asian varieties have a denser texture and hold their shape when cooked.
In Japanese cuisine pears are often served with soy sauce and wasabi as part of sushi platters.
There are more than 300 cultivars, differing in taste, color, and size.
The skin is rich in antioxidants, so it is usually left on.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Pear makes a light snack suitable for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to pears.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying unprocessed pears, rinse them thoroughly to remove any chemical residues.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: High levels of fruit acids can cause heartburn in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pear can be eaten fresh, sliced into salads, added to smoothies, baked with honey, or used in pastries. The skin can be peeled if desired, but it holds most of the nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pears in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, preferably in a paper bag to slow ripening. At room temperature they keep for 2–3 days.
